_meta.description: Opening theory tree structure with variations for V5 Thinking Simulator
_meta.structure: Each opening has main_line + variations as sub-trees with critical positions, best/mistake moves, and deep teaching content

italian_game.name: Italian Game
italian_game.white_plan: Control the center, target f7 weakness, rapid development
italian_game.black_plan: Solid defense with d6 and Be7, or aggressive with Bc5

after_Bc4.key_decision: How to respond to Bc4 - the character of the game depends on this

d5.why_bad: Too early - after exd5 Nxd5, White has a big center
d5.consequence: After exd5 Nxd5 Nxd5 Qxd5 Nc3, the queen must retreat and White has excellent development
d5.learning: In the Italian, control the center with pieces first (Bc5 or Nf6), not pawns

f6.consequence: After Nxe5! fxe5, Qh5+ wins material
f6.learning: Never play f6 in the opening - it invites tactics on the king

giuoco_piano.name: Giuoco Piano
giuoco_piano.white_plan: c3 preparing d4, control the center, rapid castling
giuoco_piano.black_plan: Solid development with d6, castle, connect rooks

after_c3.key_decision: Black must decide how to develop - d6 or Nf6

Nf6.why_good: Forces White to decide how to defend e4

d6.idea: Solid - preparing Be6 or Bg4, supports e5
d6.why_good: Controls the center with pieces, keeps tension

d5.consequence: After exd5 Nxd5, White gets d4 in comfortably
d5.learning: Keep the tension in the Italian - don't release it too early

evans_gambit.name: Evans Gambit
evans_gambit.white_plan: Sacrifice b4 pawn for rapid development and center control
evans_gambit.black_plan: Accept the gambit but develop quickly, return material if needed

key_ideas.accept: Bxb4 is critical - accept and hold if you can calculate

two_knights.name: Two Knights Defense
two_knights.white_plan: Attack with Ng5 targeting f7, or play d3 for a quiet game
two_knights.black_plan: Counter-attack! Don't be passive. d5 is the key move.

after_Ng5.key_decision: Black must react precisely to the f7 attack

d5.idea: Counter in the center! The fighting move.
d5.why_good: Opens lines, attacks the bishop, gains tempo

Bc5.why_bad: Too slow - White crashes through on f7
Bc5.consequence: Bxf7+ Ke7 and Black's king is exposed
Bc5.learning: When attacked, counter-attack! d5 is the fighting move.

common_learnings: Control the center with pieces before pawns in the Italian
The d5 break is powerful but must be timed correctly
f7 is the weak point early - defend it indirectly with development
When attacked (Ng5), counter-attack (d5) rather than defend passively

french_defense.name: French Defense
french_defense.white_plan: Space advantage with e5, attack kingside, target the weak light squares
french_defense.black_plan: Undermine White's center with c5 and f6, solve the light-squared bishop problem

after_d5.key_decision: White chooses the variation - this shapes the entire game

Nc3.name: Classical/Winawer
Nc3.idea: Develop and protect e4, main line

e5.name: Advance Variation
e5.idea: Lock the center, gain space immediately

french_advance.name: Advance Variation
french_advance.white_plan: Maintain the e5-d4 pawn chain, attack kingside with f4-f5, Bd3 battery
french_advance.black_plan: Attack the base of the chain with c5, play Nh6-f5 to pressure d4, break with f6

after_e5.key_decision: Black must immediately challenge the center

c5.idea: Attack the BASE of the pawn chain!
c5.why_good: The fundamental French principle - attack d4 to undermine e5

f6.why_bad: Too early! Weakens the kingside before developing
f6.consequence: After exf6 Nxf6, Black has wasted time and the king position is loose
f6.learning: In the French Advance, always play c5 first to attack d4. f6 comes later.

Be7.consequence: White gets a free hand to build the attack
Be7.learning: Don't develop aimlessly - challenge the opponent's strongest point

Nc6.idea: Develop and increase pressure on d4

Qb6.why_good: Forces White to make a concession

cxd4.consequence: After cxd4, White's center is stable and the c-file is less useful
cxd4.learning: Keep the tension on d4 - don't exchange unless you get something concrete

knight_maneuver.key_decision: The knight goes to h6 heading for f5

Nh6.idea: Nh6-f5 is THE key maneuver in the Advance!
Nh6.why_good: The knight on f5 pressures d4 and e3, and can't be kicked easily

french_classical.name: Classical Variation (Steinitz)
french_classical.white_plan: Push f4 to support e5, kingside attack with Qg4 or f5, restrict Black's pieces
french_classical.black_plan: Counter with c5, develop Nc6, plan f6 break, solve the light bishop problem

after_e5_Nfd7.key_decision: White must choose how to support the e5 pawn

f4.why_good: Supports e5 firmly and prepares Nf3, Be3, Qg4 attack

Nf3.why_good: Flexible - can still play f4 later

c5.why_good: Challenges d4, opens the c-file for Black's rook

f6.why_good: If timed right, opens the f-file and frees Black's position

a6.why_bad: Too slow - doesn't challenge the center
a6.learning: In the French, always prioritize center breaks (c5 or f6) over wing moves

french_winawer.name: Winawer Variation
french_winawer.white_plan: Use the bishop pair, attack kingside with Qg4 and f4, use the strong e5 pawn
french_winawer.black_plan: Target the weak c3 pawn, play Qa5, develop Ne7-f5, break with f6

after_Bb4.key_decision: The most aggressive French - Black pins the knight!

e5.why_good: Gains space and creates an asymmetric fight

after_Bxc3.key_decision: White has doubled c-pawns but the bishop pair

Ne7.idea: Head to f5 to pressure d4 and e3
Ne7.why_good: Knight on f5 is a monster

Qa5.idea: Target the weak c3 pawn immediately

Nc6.why_bad: Blocks the c-file and doesn't target c3
Nc6.consequence: White gets time to consolidate the doubled pawns
Nc6.learning: In the Winawer, the knight belongs on e7→f5, not c6

french_tarrasch.name: Tarrasch Variation
french_tarrasch.white_plan: Bd3 targets h7, Ne2-f4-g5 knight maneuver, solid center with c3
french_tarrasch.black_plan: Challenge center with c5, break with f6, develop Nc6 and Qb6

after_Nd2.key_decision: White avoids the Winawer pin with Nd2 instead of Nc3

Nf6.why_good: Forces White to push e5 or defend

french_exchange.name: Exchange Variation
french_exchange.white_plan: Minority attack with b4-b5, pressure along the e-file, exploit symmetry for first-move advantage
french_exchange.black_plan: Use the freed light bishop (Bf5 or Bg4!), central control, counterattack queenside advances

after_exd5.key_decision: Symmetrical structure - but Black's bishop is FREE!

Nf6.why_good: Prepares to castle and keeps options open

Bf5.why_good: In the Exchange, Black's light bishop is GOOD - use it!

Bd6.consequence: Makes it harder to develop the queenside
Bd6.learning: Don't block your own pawns - develop knights before bishops in symmetric positions

common_learnings: The French bishop on c8 is the 'problem piece' - always have a plan to activate it
c5 attacks the base of White's pawn chain - this is THE key break for Black
f6 is thematic but must be timed carefully - not too early, not too late
In the Advance, Nh6-f5 is the key knight maneuver
In the Winawer, target the doubled c-pawns with Qa5
In the Exchange, your light bishop is FREE - use it!

queens_gambit.name: Queen's Gambit
queens_gambit.white_plan: Central control, queenside space, minority attack or central break e4
queens_gambit.black_plan: Solid defense of d5, counterattack with c5 or e5 when ready

after_c4.key_decision: The most important decision - accept, decline, or play the Slav?

e6.name: Queen's Gambit Declined
e6.idea: Solid defense of d5, classical approach

dxc4.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted
dxc4.idea: Take the pawn but give it back for activity

c6.name: Slav Defense
c6.idea: Support d5 while keeping the bishop free!

e5.consequence: White wins a clean pawn with a better position
e5.learning: Don't try to gambit back in the Queen's Gambit - just defend d5

Nc6.consequence: Black can never play c5 or c6 to support the center
Nc6.learning: In d4 openings, keep the c-pawn free to support your center

qgd_orthodox.name: Queen's Gambit Declined (Orthodox)
qgd_orthodox.white_plan: Minority attack (a3, b4, b5) to create queenside weaknesses, control c-file
qgd_orthodox.black_plan: Solid center with c6, develop Nd7, plan c5 or e5 break, solve the bishop problem

after_Bg5.key_decision: The Bg5 pin is annoying - how to deal with it?

Be7.why_good: Prepares to castle, keeps structure intact

h6.why_good: Forces Bh4 where g5 becomes possible later

Nbd7.why_bad: Doesn't address the pin on f6
Nbd7.learning: Address pins before they become a problem. Be7 breaks the pin cleanly.

minority_attack.key_decision: White starts the minority attack - Black must know how to respond

a5.idea: Stop b4! Prevent the minority attack
a5.why_good: Fixes the queenside pawns and stops White's main plan

Ne4.why_good: Active piece play to distract from the queenside

qga.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted
qga.white_plan: Recover the pawn with Bxc4, build a strong center with e4, dominate the center
qga.black_plan: Quick development, strike with c5, expand with a6-b5, Bb7 on the long diagonal

after_dxc4.key_decision: Should Black try to hold the pawn?

Nf6.idea: Develop first, give back the pawn when ready
Nf6.why_good: Time is more important than one pawn

e6.idea: Solid approach, prepare to return the pawn
e6.why_good: Opens the bishop and supports d5

b5.why_bad: Trying to hold the c4 pawn costs too much time
b5.consequence: After a4 b4, Black's queenside is shattered
b5.learning: In the QGA, NEVER try to hold the pawn. Develop, give it back, and get active.

c5.why_good: Opens lines, activates pieces, challenges White's center

slav.name: Slav Defense
slav.white_plan: Recover the c4 pawn with a4 preventing b5, build strong center with e4
slav.black_plan: Develop Bf5 BEFORE e6 (key Slav idea!), solid structure, flexible development

after_c6.key_decision: The brilliant idea behind the Slav

Bf5.idea: THE point of the Slav - bishop comes out before e6!
Bf5.why_good: Solves the French bishop problem. The bishop is active on f5.

dxc4.idea: Take first, then develop the bishop

e6.why_bad: Defeats the purpose of the Slav!
e6.consequence: The light bishop is stuck behind the e6 pawn, just like in the French
e6.learning: The WHOLE POINT of c6 instead of e6 is to keep Bf5 available. Don't play e6 before the bishop is out!

common_learnings: The Queen's Gambit is not a real gambit - White usually gets the pawn back
In the QGD, the minority attack (b4-b5) is White's main plan
In the QGA, never try to hold the c4 pawn - develop instead
In the Slav, develop Bf5 BEFORE playing e6 - that's the whole point
c5 is Black's key break in almost all Queen's Gambit lines

london_system.name: London System
london_system.white_plan: Solid development: Bf4, e3, Nf3, Bd3, c3, Nbd2 - then push e4
london_system.black_plan: Challenge with c5 or Bd6, fight for the center, don't let White play e4 easily

after_Bf4.key_decision: Black must decide how to challenge the London setup

Bf5.idea: Mirror the London! Develop the bishop early

e6.why_bad: Passive - locks in the light bishop like the French
e6.consequence: White gets a comfortable position with easy development
e6.learning: Against the London, be active! Challenge the center or develop actively.

london_main.name: London Main Line
london_main.white_plan: Complete development with e3, Nf3, Bd3, c3, Nbd2, O-O - then push e4 when ready
london_main.black_plan: Play c5 to challenge d4, develop Bd6 to trade the London bishop, prepare e5 or dxc3

after_e3.key_decision: White has set up the London pyramid - how to respond?

c5.why_good: Prevents White from getting a free center

Bd6.why_good: After Bxd6 Qxd6, Black has the pair and targets h2

Bg4.why_bad: The pin on f3 can be broken with Be2 or h3
Bg4.consequence: After h3 Bh5, White gains time and the bishop is offside
Bg4.learning: Against the London, focus on center play (c5) rather than pins

ne5_outpost.key_decision: White's knight reaches the powerful e5 outpost

Ne5.idea: The dream square for the London knight!
Ne5.why_good: Controls c4, d3, f3, and g4 - very hard to dislodge

Nxe5.why_good: Don't let the knight sit on e5 forever

london_c5.name: London vs Early c5
london_c5.white_plan: Hold d4 with c3, develop normally, push e4 when the center is stable
london_c5.black_plan: Pressure d4 with c5 and Nc6, Qb6 targets b2, play for queenside activity

after_Qb6.key_decision: Black hits b2 and d4 simultaneously

Qb3.idea: Trade queens to neutralize the pressure
Qb3.why_good: Simplifies and removes the Qb6 threat

Qc1.idea: Keep queens on but defend b2

common_learnings: In the London, ALWAYS play Bf4 BEFORE e3 - otherwise the bishop gets trapped
The pawn triangle c3-d4-e3 is the London's fortress
Ne5 is the dream square - aim for it with Nf3-e5
Against the London, Black should play c5 early to challenge d4
If Black plays Bd6, White should trade (Bxd6) or retreat (Bg3) - don't lose the bishop pair for nothing

sicilian_dragon.name: Sicilian Dragon
sicilian_dragon.white_plan: Yugoslav Attack: castle queenside, launch h4-h5 pawn storm
sicilian_dragon.black_plan: Fianchetto bishop, counter on the c-file, attack White's king

dragon_setup.key_decision: White chooses between Yugoslav Attack (Be3, f3, Qd2, O-O-O) or Classical (Be2, O-O)

Be3.idea: Yugoslav Attack - the sharpest and most critical

yugoslav_attack.name: Yugoslav Attack
yugoslav_attack.white_plan: h4-h5-hxg6 pawn storm, Bh6 to trade dragons, g4-g5 to open lines
yugoslav_attack.black_plan: Rc8, Qa5 or Qb6, pressure on c-file, Ne5-c4 maneuver

after_O-O-O.key_decision: The race begins - who attacks faster?

Rc8.idea: The most important move - pressure the c-file
Rc8.why_good: Prepares Qa5 or Ne5-c4, creates threats against White's king

Qa5.idea: Target the a2 pawn and create threats
Qa5.why_good: Combines with Rc8 for devastating pressure

a6.why_bad: Too slow - White's attack arrives first
a6.consequence: h4-h5 comes with devastating effect before Black is ready
a6.learning: In the Dragon Yugoslav, every tempo matters - activate with Rc8 immediately

common_learnings: The Dragon is a race - whoever attacks first usually wins
Black's counterplay is on the c-file, not the a or b files
Trading the dragon bishop (Bg7) is often bad for Black
Rc8 is almost always the right move after castling

caro_kann.name: Caro-Kann Defense
caro_kann.white_plan: Build a strong center, use space advantage, attack with Nc3 or Nd2 systems
caro_kann.black_plan: Solid structure with d5, develop the light bishop to f5 or g4 BEFORE e6

caro_classical.name: Classical Variation
caro_classical.white_plan: Drive the bishop with h4-h5, control the center, develop with Nf3 and Bd3
caro_classical.black_plan: Get Bf5 out immediately (the whole point!), solid development, castle kingside

after_Nxe4.key_decision: THIS is the moment - develop the bishop!

Bf5.idea: The BEST move - develop the bishop before e6!
Bf5.why_good: This is why Black played c6 instead of e6. The bishop is active on f5.

Nd7.why_good: Prepares Ngf6 but doesn't solve the bishop problem yet

e6.why_bad: Defeats the purpose of the Caro-Kann!
e6.consequence: The light bishop is stuck behind the pawn chain, like in the French
e6.learning: In the Caro-Kann, the bishop goes to f5 BEFORE you play e6. That's the whole point of c6.

caro_advance.name: Advance Variation
caro_advance.white_plan: Maintain the e5 space advantage, develop smoothly, kingside attack potential
caro_advance.black_plan: Develop Bf5 first, then challenge with c5 and f6, castle and counterattack

after_e5.key_decision: The center is locked - bishop first!

Bf5.idea: Get the bishop out before e6 locks it in!
Bf5.why_good: Active bishop on f5, then e6, then challenge with c5

e6.learning: In the Caro-Kann Advance, ALWAYS play Bf5 before e6

common_learnings: Get the light-squared bishop out before playing e6 - this is the Caro-Kann's superpower
The pawn structure is solid - don't rush to create weaknesses
c5 is often a key break in the middlegame to challenge d4
The endgame is often favorable for Black due to the solid, no-weakness structure

sicilian_najdorf.name: Sicilian Najdorf
sicilian_najdorf.white_plan: Attack! Choose between Be2 (English Attack), Bg5 (main line), f3 (English Attack), or Bc4
sicilian_najdorf.black_plan: Fight for counterplay with e5, b5, or Bb7. The most dynamic Black opening.

after_a6.key_decision: White must choose their weapon - each leads to a completely different game

Be2.name: Classical/English Attack
Be2.idea: Flexible - can lead to f4 and Be3 setups

Bg5.name: Main Line
Bg5.idea: Pin the knight, prepare for sharp play

f3.name: English Attack
f3.idea: Be3, Qd2, O-O-O - full queenside castling attack

najdorf_english.name: English Attack
najdorf_english.white_plan: Castle queenside, launch g4-g5 pawn storm, attack the Black king
najdorf_english.black_plan: b5-b4 counterattack, Rc8 pressure, piece play against White's king

after_O-O-O.key_decision: The race is ON - both sides attack opposite flanks

b5.idea: Counterattack! Open lines against White's king
b5.why_good: b4 will fork the knight and open the b-file

Rc8.why_good: Doubles the threat on the c-file

common_learnings: a6 is the Najdorf move - it prevents Nb5 and prepares b5 expansion
e5 is the key central break for Black in most Najdorf lines
The Najdorf is a FIGHTING opening - don't play it if you want a quiet game
Both sides often castle on opposite wings, leading to a race

ruy_lopez.name: Ruy Lopez (Spanish Opening)
ruy_lopez.white_plan: Pressure e5 indirectly through the Nc6 pin, build a strong center with d4
ruy_lopez.black_plan: Defend with a6 and b5, maintain the center, develop actively

after_Bb5.key_decision: How to handle the pin on Nc6

a6.name: Morphy Defense
a6.idea: Challenge the bishop - the main line

d6.why_bad: Too passive - doesn't challenge the bishop
d6.consequence: White gets a comfortable advantage with d4
d6.learning: Always challenge the Bb5 with a6 - make the bishop decide

morphy_defense.name: Morphy Defense
morphy_defense.white_plan: d4 to open the center, build pressure with Re1, Bc2, d4
morphy_defense.black_plan: The Breyer/Chigorin maneuver: Nb8-d7, Bb7, Re8, Bf8

after_O-O_Be7.key_decision: Black prepares to castle - the long strategic battle begins

b5.idea: Push the bishop back and gain space
b5.why_good: Prepares d6, Bb7, and a long-term position

d6.why_good: Classical approach, keeps all options open

common_learnings: Bb5 doesn't actually threaten to win e5 (Bxc6 dxc6, Nxe5? Qd4 wins it back)
a6 challenges the bishop and is almost always the right response
The Ruy Lopez is a long strategic battle - don't expect quick tactics
Black's Breyer maneuver (Nb8-d7) is one of the deepest ideas in chess
